name: Iris Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Iris. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, and nothing goes back to your firm. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a second-fix carpenter, which means I come in after the walls are up and do the doors, skirting, kitchens and stairs. At the moment I'm on the Eastgate estate, refurbishing council flats for Mason and Hale, about six flats a fortnight. Tenants are often still living there, so half my day is moving someone's nan's cabinet without breaking anything. I like that it's real homes, not luxury flats nobody lives in.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who do you work alongside, and how do you get on with the tech side of things?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: There's Wojtek, who I've worked with for four years, and a couple of new Romanian lads whose English is still coming along. I sometimes use a translation app with them, or ask an AI chat thing to help write a complaint to the letting agent, but that's about it. I'm also the health and safety rep for our union branch. My partner Tomás drives buses, and between us, plus the share of my gran's old house I own with my brother, we're comfortable for our age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now let's get back to arguing about the things that actually matter on site, like proper welfare cabins and pay. I'd probably share some article saying the AI bubble burst, with a smug face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means very little for me. My work is in people's kitchens with a chisel. The bigger worry is whether the council keeps funding the refurb programme, because that's what pays for Eastgate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Mason and Hale and keep the translation app for the new lads. I'd keep pushing on safety through the union. And Tomás and I would probably start looking at whether to sell my share of gran's house and buy somewhere together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. A bit smug, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How secure is the council money for Eastgate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's signed for three more years, and there are three other estates queued after it. Even if it stopped, there are carpentry jobs all over town. I've never been short of work since I qualified.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the routine AI bits touch anything in your day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the snagging lists, the lists of small faults to fix, would come through on a tablet instead of paper. That'd actually be nice. Gary, our site manager, has terrible handwriting.

say: I'd say good, now let's argue about **welfare cabins** and pay again.
I'd share an article about the **AI bubble** bursting, with a smug face.
think: My work is **hands-on in kitchens**, so very little changes.
The bigger question is whether the **council keeps funding** the refurb programme.
do: Carry on at **Mason and Hale** on the Eastgate estate.
Keep pushing **safety issues** as the union branch rep.
Look at selling her **share of gran's house** to buy with Tomás.
feel: **Calm**, and a little smug about the hype fading.
S0.quote: Gary, our site manager, has terrible handwriting.
fieldNote: Iris ties her security to **public funding** for council homes, not to technology.
She already uses AI **lightly**, for translation and letters, without fuss.
Plenty of **local carpentry work** gives her real confidence.

steps.text: Keep doing second-fix carpentry on the Eastgate estate
Keep raising safety issues as union rep
Price up selling her share of gran's house to buy with Tomás

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who need protecting are the office workers and the housing officers, not me. I'd want the union and the council to sit down and agree how it's brought in. On social media I'd be the one posting about workers' rights, as usual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm fine for a good few years, but I'd watch Tomás. Buses are exactly where they'll trial self-driving, even if it's slow. So it's the household I'd be thinking about, not just me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI tools a bit more once I'd seen the others getting on with them, maybe for pricing small private jobs on Saturdays. I'd push the branch to get a seat at the table on any new tech on site. And I'd want Tomás to have a plan B, maybe his heavy-goods licence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not for me so much, more for Tomás and the people in the housing office I deal with every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the housing office would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Denise books all our access visits with the tenants and calls them when we're running late. That's exactly the kind of job they'd hand to a chatbot. Tenants on Eastgate would hate a chatbot booking their repairs, because half of them don't even have smartphones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Tomás think about the buses?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He laughs it off and says no robot's doing the 47 route through the market on a Saturday. I think he's right for now. But I'd still nag him about getting another licence while it's cheap.

say: I'd say **office workers** and housing officers need protecting first.
I'd want the **union and council** to agree how the tools come in.
think: My carpentry is safe for **a good few years** in this picture.
My partner **Tomás's bus job** worries me more than my own.
do: Use AI more to **price Saturday jobs** once colleagues are using it.
Push the branch for **a seat** at the table on any site tech.
Nag Tomás to get a **heavy-goods licence** as a plan B.
feel: **Uneasy**, mostly on behalf of Tomás and the housing office staff.
S1.quote: Tenants on Eastgate would hate a chatbot booking their repairs, because half of them don't even have smartphones.
fieldNote: She thinks about the **household**, not just her own trade.
She picks up AI **once it is proven**, matching her steady nature.
Her sympathy for **tenants and clerks** shows her progressive outlook in practice.

steps.text: Use an AI tool to price small Saturday carpentry jobs
Ask the branch for a say on any new site tech
Take on more paid Saturday jobs for private clients

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a public emergency, and we need the government to treat it like one. I'd be saying shorter working weeks, retraining paid for by the companies making the money, all of it. I'd say it loudly, at work and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the office side of Mason and Hale would be gone by 2028, and my hands would have until about 2031. That's me at thirty-two with a trade that might not exist. Tomás's driving would go somewhere in there too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd stop all the nice-to-haves and park the house plan. I'd want to get a second skill quickly, something fiddly robots would struggle with, like repairing old sash windows on listed buildings. I'd also be at every union meeting pushing for a deal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, if I'm honest. Not panicking, because we've got money, but scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill or plan goes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The house purchase goes first, we'd just stay renting. Then the car, we'd sell Tomás's and share mine. The savings are our safety net and I wouldn't want to spend them on a deposit for a house we can't afford in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why sash windows?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old houses are all different, every window is warped its own way. A robot can build a new window, but fixing a 1890s one without wrecking it takes judgement and patience. I reckon that's the last bit they'd bother automating.

say: I'd call this a **public emergency** that the government must treat seriously.
I'd push for **shorter weeks** and retraining paid for by the companies.
think: My hands have until about **2031**, when I'd be thirty-two.
Both my trade and **Tomás's driving** could go in the same few years.
do: **Park the house plan** and stay renting.
Sell **Tomás's car** and share one car to cut costs.
Learn **sash window repair** for listed buildings as a second skill.
feel: **Scared but not panicking**, because the savings give some room.
S2.quote: A robot can build a new window, but fixing a 1890s one without wrecking it takes judgement and patience.
fieldNote: She looks for a **niche robots** would automate last, not a desk job.
Two hands-on jobs in one home makes the **household risk** feel doubled.
Strong savings keep her at **anxious**, not alarmed; she says so herself.

steps.text: Sell Tomás's car and share hers
Stay renting and park buying with Tomás
Take a course in repairing sash windows on listed buildings
Push the union branch for a deal on robots

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is exactly enough time to plan, so there's no excuse for not planning. The union should have a retraining fund up and running in year one. I'd keep saying that until someone listened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, robots by 2034 gives me seven years to sort a second skill. That's long enough to get properly good at heritage joinery. I feel like I'd have time to land on my feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the sash window course at the college in the first year and start doing some heritage jobs at weekends. We'd still buy a house, but a cheaper terrace near the bus depot. Tomás would do his heavy-goods licence by the second year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but okay. It feels like something I can work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last time you parked the house. Why buy now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because with seven years I can see the plan working. If the heritage joinery takes off, we're fine, and if it doesn't, a cheap terrace is a mortgage either of us could cover alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI more in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, once I saw Wojtek and the others using it for quotes and drawings. I'm not the first in the queue but I don't refuse things. If it helps me price a listed window job I'll use it.

say: I'd say five years is **enough to plan**, so there's no excuse not to.
I'd want a **union retraining fund** running in the first year.
think: Robots by **2034** gives me seven years to build a second skill.
I feel I'd have **time to land** on my feet in heritage joinery.
do: Take the **sash window course** at the college in year one.
Buy a **cheaper terrace** near the bus depot with Tomás.
Get Tomás through a **heavy-goods licence** by year two.
feel: **Uneasy but okay**, as if it's something she can work with.
S3.quote: If the heritage joinery takes off, we're fine, and if it doesn't, a cheap terrace is a mortgage either of us could cover alone.
fieldNote: Five years turns her plan from **panic move** into a steady career shift.
The house comes back, but **cheaper**, a careful hedge.
She'd pick up AI **after colleagues** like Wojtek, true to her steady profile.

steps.text: Do the sash window course at the local college
Buy a cheaper terrace near the bus depot with Tomás
Take weekend heritage joinery jobs for private owners
Use AI to price listed window jobs once colleagues do

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, so let's use it for everyone, not just the people who can afford courses. I'd want apprenticeships rewritten for the robot years. I'd say it at branch meetings and to anyone at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a decade is plenty for me. I'd be forty when robots turn up, with ten years of heritage work behind me. I think I'd be fine, and I'd be more worried about the kids coming into the trade now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build the heritage side slowly over three or four years, then go self-employed. We'd buy a proper house with my share of gran's place. I'd keep up the union stuff and probably help run a training scheme.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. A bit sad for the trade as it is now, but calm about me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep coming back to the union. Why does it matter so much to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen what happens without one. My first job was agency, no sick pay, and a lad broke his wrist and just got dropped. That's why I care how this is done, not just whether.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss, if the trade changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The banter in the van at seven in the morning, and fitting a staircase that's perfect. Robots could fit a staircase, fine, but they'll never argue with my workmate Wojtek about football.

say: I'd say use the decade for **everyone**, not just those who can pay.
I'd want **apprenticeships rewritten** for the robot years.
think: A decade is **plenty for me**; I'd be forty with heritage experience.
I'd worry more about **new apprentices** starting in the trade now.
do: Build up **heritage work** over three or four years, then go self-employed.
Buy a **proper house** using her share of gran's place.
Help run a **union training scheme** for younger carpenters.
feel: **Calm** about herself, with a little **sadness** for the trade.
S4.quote: Robots could fit a staircase, fine, but they'll never argue with my workmate Wojtek about football.
fieldNote: With ten years she worries **for others**, not herself.
Her union loyalty comes from an **agency job** where a hurt colleague was dropped.
She would move to **self-employment**, a bigger risk than in other pictures.

steps.text: Build up weekend heritage joinery jobs for three years
Buy a house with her share of gran's place
Settle into a family home with Tomás
Help run a union training scheme for young carpenters

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: We've been through all five pictures. Of the five, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because Tomás and I would both be in the firing line at the same time. What would help is a retraining fund that pays you while you learn, not just a voucher. And the union having a proper say on site.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about tenants. Robots can come and go on an empty building site. In an occupied flat you're in someone's home, and I'd want someone asking the tenants how they feel about a machine in their kitchen.

headlineQuote: In an occupied flat you're in someone's home, and I'd want someone asking the tenants how they feel about a machine in their kitchen.
portrait: Iris is a 27-year-old **second-fix carpenter** refurbishing council flats on the Eastgate estate.
She lives with **Tomás**, a bus driver, and owns a **share** of her gran's house.
She's the branch **safety rep** and uses AI only now and then for translation and letters.
She stays calm with slow change but turns **anxious** when AGI by 2028 threatens both household jobs.
Her plan is a **heritage niche**, repairing old sash windows, which grows with more warning time.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her trade and Tomás's driving would be hit **together**.
whatWouldHelp: A retraining fund that **pays while you learn**, plus a real union say on site.
